html:
The Tutelo were a Native American people of the Piedmont in what is now Virginia and West Virginia, living above the fall line of the rivers. They called themselves Yesáh. Their language belonged to the Ohio Valley branch of the Siouan family, making them distant relatives of the Siouan peoples of the Plains.

They lived in farming villages, growing maize, beans and squash, and hunted in the hills. English explorers from Virginia reached them in the 1670s.

Pressed by English settlers and by raids of the Haudenosaunee from the north, in the late 1600s they joined related peoples such as the Saponi; together they were known as the Nahyssan. By 1740 they had to leave their homeland, and they moved north to seek protection from their former enemies. In 1753 the Cayuga formally adopted them. After the American Revolution their descendants moved with the Haudenosaunee to the Six Nations of the Grand River in Ontario. Their southern neighbours had included the Catawba.
